title: Updating plans and communicating change
blurb: Explain why plans, schedules and records must be updated to reflect an approved change, and how to communicate it to everyone affected.
question: The sponsor has approved Millbrook's CR-031: build the platform 2 lift shaft now. It adds about two weeks and £120k. Before the contractor starts, what must the project manager update, who needs to be told, and why does it matter?

teach.body: Once a change is approved, the plans and schedules are updated so the baseline stays accurate and everyone works to the same version. The change and its effects are then communicated to every stakeholder it affects. In plain English: the paperwork catches up with the decision before the work does, and nobody is surprised. This is the update plans stage, and it comes before implement.

teach.caption: Because the plans are integrated, a change to one (the schedule) is reflected in the others (budget, resources, risks).
Progress is now measured against week 32. Reporting against the old week 30 would show a false delay.

teach.body: If the baseline is not updated, progress reports compare actual work with a plan that no longer exists: approved spend looks like an overspend and an agreed delay looks like slippage. Teams may build from superseded drawings. New risks go unowned. Stakeholders keep planning around old dates. An accurate, updated baseline keeps monitoring and control meaningful, supports governance and the audit trail, and keeps everyone's expectations aligned.

teach.h: Who needs to know about CR-031
head: Stakeholder
What they need to know
How
teach.caption: Tailor the message to each stakeholder: what changed, why, how it affects them and what they need to do.
Communication continues through implementation, and the request is closed in the change log once the change is delivered.

teach.body: In a linear life cycle, an approved change means formally rebaselining: a new schedule and budget, a new version of the project management plan approved by the sponsor, and new configuration item versions issued. In an iterative life cycle, most changes are reflected by reordering the backlog and updating the release and time-box plans, made visible on team boards and shared at reviews and planning sessions. If a change alters the fixed time or cost, the higher-level plan and baseline are updated formally too.

teach.text: Exam traps: 'start the work now and tidy up the plans later' (update plans comes BEFORE implement); 'only the schedule needs updating' (budget, risk register, configuration records and the PMP too); and 'telling the sponsor is enough' (every affected stakeholder needs to know, in a form that suits them).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Update the baseline (scope, schedule, budget) so progress is measured against the agreed plan.
Update the PMP and related plans so they stay integrated and consistent.
Update configuration records, the risk register and the change log status.
Communicate what changed, why and its effects to all affected stakeholders.
Result: one version of the truth, no false variances, no surprises.
Update plans and schedules so the baseline stays accurate and everyone works to the same version.
Update the PMP, configuration records, risk register, budget and change log too.
Out-of-date baselines create false variances, rework and unmanaged risks.
Communicate the change and its effects to every affected stakeholder, tailored to them.
Linear: formal rebaselining. Iterative: backlog and release plan updated, formal if time or cost change.

summary: You can now explain why plans, schedules and records must be updated after a change is approved, and what goes wrong if they are not. You can also say how to communicate the change to everyone affected, and how updating differs in linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: What is the main reason for updating the baseline after a change has been approved?
options: So the change no longer needs any approval
So progress is tracked against the new plan
So the sponsor is able to reverse the decision
So the risk register can be closed down
A.why: An updated baseline means progress, cost and dates are measured against the plan that now includes the approved change.

whyNot.0: The change has already been approved; updating the baseline puts that decision into effect.
whyNot.2: Updating plans is not a route to reversing a decision.
whyNot.3: The risk register is updated with new risks, not closed.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT usually updated as a result of an approved project change?
options: The configuration records
The project risk register
The organisation's strategy
The project budget baseline
A.why: A single project change does not alter the organisation's strategy. The other three are typically updated.

whyNot.0: Configuration records are updated so the current versions are clear.
whyNot.1: The risk register is updated with new or changed risks.
whyNot.3: The budget is updated to include any approved extra cost.

A.q: Who should be told about an approved change and its effects?
options: All the stakeholders it affects
Only the sponsor who approved it
Only the team that will build it
Only the person who requested it
A.why: Everyone affected by the change needs to know what changed, why and how it affects them.

whyNot.1: The sponsor already knows; others affected still need to be told.
whyNot.2: The team needs to know, but so do the other affected stakeholders.
whyNot.3: The requester should be told, but they are not the only one affected.

B.q: Two weeks after CR-031 is approved, the contractor is found building to drawing revision B, although revision C reflects the change. What is the most likely cause?
options: The change was rejected by the sponsor
The detailed evaluation was not done
The requester withdrew their request
Records and drawings were not reissued
B.why: The configuration records and drawings were not updated and communicated, so the contractor is working from a superseded version.

whyNot.0: The change was approved; the problem is what happened afterwards.
whyNot.1: The evaluation happened; the failure is in updating and communicating plans.
whyNot.2: A withdrawn request would not lead to a new drawing revision.

B.q: A month after a £120k change is approved, the progress report shows a £120k overspend and a red status. What is the most likely cause?
options: The budget baseline was not updated
The change was not needed after all
The contractor has overcharged
The sponsor never approved it
B.why: If the budget baseline is not updated for the approved change, the agreed extra spend shows up as a false overspend.

whyNot.1: Whether it was needed was settled at the decision; it does not explain the reporting.
whyNot.2: Overcharging is possible, but an exact match to the approved amount points to an unchanged baseline.
whyNot.3: The scenario says the change was approved.

B.q: On an iterative project, how is an accepted scope change usually reflected in the plans?
options: The business case is fully rewritten
Nothing changes until the very final release
The backlog and release plan are updated
A new contract is signed with the team
B.why: In iterative work the backlog is reordered and the release and time-box plans updated, then shared at reviews and planning.

whyNot.0: A routine scope change does not require rewriting the business case.
whyNot.1: Changes are reflected straight away in the backlog so the next time box is planned correctly.
whyNot.3: Prioritisation changes do not need a new contract.

C.q: CR-031 moves Millbrook's handover from week 30 to week 32. Station staff rotas and a passenger information campaign are planned around the handover date. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep week 30 in reports to avoid alarm
Update the schedule and tell those teams
Tell only the sponsor and leave the rest
Wait until handover to explain the delay
C.why: The schedule must reflect the approved change, and the teams whose plans depend on the date must be told so they can adjust.

whyNot.0: Reporting a superseded date creates false information and later surprises.
whyNot.2: Other affected stakeholders also need to know.
whyNot.3: Leaving it late removes their chance to replan, damaging trust.

C.q: Which THREE should normally be updated after a change is approved? 1. The schedule 2. The risk register 3. The configuration records 4. The lessons log of a finished project
options: 1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 3
C.why: The schedule (1), risk register (2) and configuration records (3) are all updated. A finished project's lessons log (4) is unaffected.

whyNot.0: A finished project's lessons log (4) is not changed, and this misses configuration records (3).
whyNot.1: A finished project's lessons log (4) is not changed, and this misses the schedule (1).
whyNot.2: A finished project's lessons log (4) is not changed, and this misses the risk register (2).

C.q: Why does having an integrated project management plan help when updating for an approved change?
options: A change in one plan carries through all
It removes the need to tell stakeholders
It means only the schedule needs a change
It lets the team skip configuration control
C.why: An integrated plan links the subsidiary plans, so a schedule change is reflected in the budget, resources, risks and communications.

whyNot.1: Stakeholders still need to be told.
whyNot.2: Integration means more plans are kept consistent, not fewer updated.
whyNot.3: Configuration control still applies to the updated items.

reteach.title: Think of a school timetable
reteach.question: A school agrees to move the science block's opening from September to October. What has to change on paper, and who has to be told, before term starts?

blocks.h: Change the timetable, then tell everyone
blocks.body: The head approves the later date. Before term, the timetable is redrawn so science runs in temporary rooms in September, the budget shows the extra hire cost, the room booking system shows the new rooms, and the risk list notes the crowded corridors. Then everyone affected is told: teachers get new timetables, parents get a letter, the caretaker gets new opening times. If only the head knew, chemistry classes would turn up at a locked building.

blocks.text: Updating the timetable but not telling anyone is as bad as telling everyone but never updating the timetable. You need both.

explain.body: The baseline (scope, schedule and budget), the project management plan, configuration records (new versions of affected items), the risk register and the change log status. Because the plans are integrated, each update is carried through to the others.

test.q: Besides the schedule, which are typically updated after a change is approved?
options: The organisation's annual accounts
The previous project's closure report
The risk register and the budget
The sponsor's job description
test.why: The risk register and budget are updated alongside the schedule, PMP and configuration records.

whyNot.0: Annual accounts are an organisational matter, not a project plan.
whyNot.1: Another project's closure report is not affected.
whyNot.3: A change request does not alter the sponsor's role description.

explain.body: Monitoring compares actual progress with the baseline. If the baseline does not include approved changes, the variances are false: approved cost looks like overspend, agreed delay looks like slippage, and decisions are made on wrong information.

test.q: If the baseline is not updated for an approved change, what happens to progress reporting?
options: It becomes more accurate over time
The variances shown are misleading
It no longer needs to be produced
It switches to the iterative style
test.why: Reports compare actuals with an out-of-date plan, so variances do not reflect real performance.

whyNot.0: Accuracy gets worse, not better, as actuals drift from the old plan.
whyNot.2: Reporting is still required; it just becomes unreliable.
whyNot.3: The life cycle approach does not change because a baseline was not updated.

explain.body: Tell every affected stakeholder what changed, why, how it affects them and what they need to do. Tailor the message and channel to each audience, use the communication plan, and check it has been understood.

test.q: A good communication about an approved change tells stakeholders…
options: only the new end date of the project
the full detailed evaluation report
who first asked for the change and the reason
what changed, why and how it affects them
test.why: Stakeholders need to know what changed, why, and what it means for them, so they can adjust their own plans.

whyNot.0: The end date alone leaves out the reason and other effects.
whyNot.1: Most stakeholders need a tailored summary, not the full report.
whyNot.2: Who asked is less important than what the change means for them.

explain.body: Linear: formal rebaselining, a new approved PMP version and new configuration item versions. Iterative: the backlog and release or time-box plans are updated and shared at reviews and planning; formal updates are made if fixed time or cost change.

test.q: On a linear project, updating plans after an approved change usually involves…
options: rebaselining and a new approved PMP version
reordering the backlog for the next time box
waiting until handover to revise the plans
replacing the business case with a new one
test.why: Linear projects formally rebaseline and issue a new, approved version of the project management plan.

whyNot.1: Backlog reordering is the iterative approach.
whyNot.2: Plans are updated before implementation, not at handover.
whyNot.3: The business case may be reviewed, but it is not simply replaced.
